event: Nala stands up at the trestle and sings "O Danny Boy", slow and low, for the room.

changes.note: Nala's first singing here starts a practice tally; a quarter hour banks no point yet

event: The voice that comes out is not the one she left behind; she has to find it as she goes.
The tune is nothing Harrow knows. Ned Fuller the smith sets his cup down to listen.

memory.fact: The Sheaf's regulars are Ned Fuller the smith, Hattie Rook, and the Cranes' two hands.

event: Every word lands: a farewell, someone gone away, a promise to be there when they come home.

memory.fact: Harrow folk understand every word Nala sings; it is the song itself that is new to them.
Harrow folk understand every word Nala sings; it is the song itself that is new to them.

event: A lad at the far trestle stops chewing. Martha's ladle hangs over the pot.
On the high climb of the chorus her new voice cracks, and she has to drop under the note.

memory.fact: Nala's new voice is not Alan's; it cracked on a high chorus and she had to drop under the note.
Nala's new voice is not Alan's; it cracked on a high chorus and she had to drop under the note.

event: She finds it again for the last lines, and holds the last note and lets it die out.
Nobody claps. They knock the trestles with their knuckles, which is what Harrow does.

memory.fact: Harrow folk do not clap; they knock the trestles with their knuckles.
Harrow folk do not clap; they knock the trestles with their knuckles.

event: She goes straight on into "Homeward Bound", a plainer song, faster, about going home.
It is a stranger's song about a stranger far from home, sung by a stranger with no home to name.
Hattie Rook leans to the woman beside her and whispers, eyes on Nala's bare feet.
Nala reaches the last verse, about wanting to be home, and her voice scrapes on it.
She finishes with her throat raw and her hands not quite steady, in a body that isn't hers.

memory.fact: On day one's evening Nala sang O Danny Boy and Homeward Bound in the Sheaf.

event: Aldous hasn't moved from the door, and his face has gone still the way it went still at her name.

memory.fact: Aldous stood by the Sheaf's door through Nala's songs, his face gone still as at her name.
Aldous stood by the Sheaf's door through Nala's songs, his face gone still as at her name.

event: The room is pleased with her and uneasy about her at once, and neither feeling wins.

memory.fact: The Sheaf's room was pleased with Nala's singing and uneasy about her at once.
The Sheaf's room was pleased with Nala's singing and uneasy about her at once.

event: Martha breaks it. "Well. The lass can sing." She hooks a stool out from under the next trestle.

make.title: Nala and Martha Deane
make.description: How far the Sheaf's keeper regards Nala.

changes.note: Nala sings for Martha's room, and a bond with her starts at nothing
Word kept, respect and aid: she sang at once, and gave the Sheaf two songs

event: Coppers go down on the wood: three of them, from Ned and Hattie and a hand at the back.

changes.note: Three coppers left on the trestle for her songs

memory.fact: The Sheaf's folk pay a singer in coppers left on the trestle, one or two apiece.
The Sheaf's folk pay a singer in coppers left on the trestle, one or two apiece.

event: The question the whole room is holding comes out of the back: "Where'd you learn songs like that?"
Martha sets a cup in front of her. "Another. Then you'll say where a girl gets songs like that."

memory.fact: After Nala's songs Martha said the lass can sing, and asked another, then where she got such songs.
